seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: A Gap in the Glass
blurb: Ada has half a name and sixteen shards on the bench. At ninth bell, with Emrys keeping the record, she mends. Some things come back with a gap in them.

blocks.text: Ninth bell, slow and deep across the water, and rain coming sideways at the shop window.

Sixteen shards lay on the bench in a ragged ring. Over them the readout hung pale gold: WICK, and under it, INCOMPLETE. A line of light ran edge to edge through every piece, then off across the bare wood, pointing at nothing.
Odile's hand drifted toward the glass.
"Don't," Ada said. Sharp. Short. "If you touch the inner glass, it's gone for good."
Odile's hand stopped in the air.
One, Ada counted. Two. Three.

"Sorry," Odile said. She had no pins in. She'd taken them out at the door, which was how Ada knew she was frightened. "Sorry. I only wanted to... it's warm, isn't it? You can feel it from here. Like a cup somebody's just put down."
On the stool by the door, Emrys Vale had the Register open on his knees and his pen lifted. "For the record," he said, "the witness notes that nobody touched anything." A pause. "Yet."

Ada had read rule six that morning at first bell, standing up, with her coat still on. Nobody touches the inner glass but you. Not during. Not ever. It goes. Underlined twice, which for the old mender was practically a whisper.
Then she'd walked round by the bridge to Cutter's Row with the ledger under her arm, and laid it open on Odile's table between the two cold cups.
"Fane, I.," Odile had read aloud. "Fane, I... Fane, Irene? Fane, Ivy? There's no I. There's me. There's only ever been..."
And she had stopped, and looked up at the hearth shelf, at the clean square in the dust.
"The glass came out of your grate," Ada had said. "The name's yours. I won't mend it without your say-so. And I'd like you there."
Odile had sat still for longer than Ada had known she could. Then she'd said, "Ninth bell. I'll bring cake." She had not brought cake.
"Right," Ada said now. "Hands in your lap, Odile. Emrys, you're holding a pen, so you're fine."
"I'm a witness," said Emrys. "Witnesses are... I was going to say impartial. I'm not. Go on."
Ada looked at the bar under the readout, empty, with its notch cut out of the far end.

Last night she'd sworn she wouldn't start a job she couldn't close. She'd stared at that notch half the night since. It wasn't a fault. It was a measurement. The readout knew exactly how much was missing and had already cut the job to fit. Fill the bar to the notch and the job was closed. Short a part, and labelled as short.
She had signed off worse. She tried not to think about when.
And she had a name now, or half of one. Fane, I. Not much. Enough to work on.
She touched the first shard.

It clicked under her finger, warm as skin. The line of light tightened, and the shards began to move. Not much. A hair's width, then another, sliding over the wood with a sound like teeth meshing in a gearbox, small and patient. Odile made a noise in her throat. Emrys's pen did not move at all.
Ada traced the light from piece to piece. The bar filled behind her finger, gold, steady, a quarter, a half.
Then the bench went away.
Rain. A window, black with night, and the room behind it warm. Ada knew the room. The stove. The table. The dummy by the window, and the soft green wool on it.
She was looking through someone else's eyes, the way she had with Tobias, with Pim. In the dark window glass a face looked back: dark hair pinned up, a wide mouth, a dimple in one cheek.
Odile's face. But not Odile.

There was a pincushion on the wrist. There was a pencil in the hand, and a slip of paper on the sill, and the pencil was writing. Ada couldn't see the words. The eyes she was borrowing wouldn't look at them.
"Somebody ought to know." The voice was Odile's, but slower, and lower. "That's all. Somebody ought to." And at the end of it, a laugh that didn't quite come off.
The paper folded once. Twice. Small. A pin came out of the cushion.
The eyes turned toward the green dress.
And there the picture ran out. Not faded. Ran out, ragged, like a page torn short. In the torn place, right at the edge, there was something dark.
A hand in a glove. Fingers closing.
Then nothing.
The bench came back hard. Ada was gripping its edge. The rain was the shop's rain again.
On the wood in front of her stood a lantern. Whole, or nearly. Low on one side the glass had a gap in it, ragged, the size of a thumbnail. Inside, a small flame burned anyway, low and steady.
The bar was full to the notch. INCOMPLETE flickered once and faded with the rest of the readout. Job closed.
Ada breathed out.
"Ines," Odile said.
She said it as if she'd been holding it in her mouth for a week and had only just remembered to swallow.

"Ines. Oh. Ines." Her hands were in her lap still, wound together. "She takes her tea black and steals my sugar anyway. Took. She took it black. She can't sew a straight hem, she pins everything, she pins her shopping list to her sleeve. We were twins. Did you know that? No, of course you didn't. Nobody did. Nobody did for a whole week."
"I didn't know," Ada said.

"The cups." Odile laughed, and it went wrong in the middle. "That's her cup. I've poured her tea every morning since Flood Night. I knew why. I always knew why, till last week. And the dress. It's her size. Our birthday. It was always her size, I've been doing ten minutes a night on it for ten years, because..." She stopped. "Because I didn't want to finish it."
Emrys had taken his spectacles off. He held them by one arm and said nothing at all.
Ada looked at the gap in the glass.
The last shard keeps the last hand.
Somebody had swept this lantern up and tipped it in the canal. And somebody had kept one piece back. Now she knew why. That piece held the hand, and whoever owned the hand wanted it kept dark.
A glove. Dark. That was all she had. It wasn't enough to say out loud, and she didn't.
"Ada." Odile was looking at her. "You saw her. In there."
"For a moment."
"What was she doing?"
"Standing at your window," Ada said. "Laughing at something."
That was true. The paper was Ines's. Whatever Ines had folded small and hidden, she'd chosen to hide it. It wasn't Ada's to unfold.
"And did you see..." Odile swallowed. "How did she die? I remember she went out. I remember the water. I don't remember the how. You saw, didn't you? Something?"
Ada thought of a long stone quay with every lamp dark, and water to the knees, and a crack of timber overhead. Two hands between a woman's shoulders. A man whispering God forgive me.
That was Tobias's. Not hers to give either.
"Flood Night," Ada said.
"I know it was Flood Night, love, I'm asking..."
"Flood Night. That's what I can tell you."
Odile looked at her for a long time. Then she nodded, slowly. "That's a no with its manners on," she said. "All right. All right. I'll take the manners."
By the door, Emrys put his spectacles back on and looked at Ada as if she were a page he'd have to read twice.
Ada waited for the cost.

She'd learned to wait for it, the way you wait for the hum after you throw a switch. She went looking. Mum's number, still four digits, no more. The knee, still a scar and no story. Then further back, further out.
Walking home from the station after a late shift. Down the steps. Left past the bus shelter. The long hill, the postbox at the top. She could see the postbox. Red, a bit dented.
After the postbox, nothing.

She knew there was a turning. She knew her own front door was at the end of it. She could not get from the one to the other. She stood at the top of a hill in her own head with the way home cut clean off.
One. Two. Three. Four.
She opened the drawer, took out the sheet of brown paper, and wrote under My knee. How.
3. The way home from the station. The last turn.
Emrys watched her write it. This time he didn't ask.

Odile had wrapped the lantern in her knitted shawl, gap side in, the way you'd tuck a sleeping child. "I'm taking her home," she said. "There's a place on the shelf that's exactly her size. I've walked past it for a week like a fool." At the door she turned back. "Thank you, Ada Brannock. That's still not a Quay name. I don't care."
The bell over the door rang, and the rain took her.
Emrys sat a moment longer. Then, carefully, he turned the pages of the Register to Cutter's Row and laid his finger under Odile's line.
Ada came round the bench to look.
Fane, Odile.
And beneath it, where the ruled line had stood empty, in brown ink gone soft with years, in a hand that wasn't his:
Fane, Ines.
Emrys did not move his finger. His finger was shaking.

"That line was blank this morning," he said. "It has been blank for... It was written ten years ago. Look at the ink. Nobody wrote it tonight. It's simply there again, as if it never..." He stopped. He started again, quieter. "Get your coat."
"It's the middle of the night."
"Yes," said Emrys. "For the record, I'd noticed."

The bridge was empty, the hot-apple woman long gone, the rail cold and wet under Ada's hand. Every lamp along the water was lit. Above the square the clock tower stood black against the fog, and its face said nothing, and its hands did not move.

The Register office was two rooms at the top of a stair off the square, in the tower's shadow. It smelled of ink and cold paper. Emrys lit the desk lamp with a taper, unlocked a drawer, and took out a single folded sheet in his own small hand.
Dates. Page numbers. A line for each.

"When I took the office," he said, "there were four blank lines in the Register. I thought they were a clerk's mistakes. Then in my first winter a fifth went. Between one evening and the next morning. A whole name, gone, and the street with it. I couldn't remember whose it had been. Nobody could." He turned the sheet so she could read it. "Since then, six more. Eleven in ten years. The last was eleven days ago." He touched the bottom line. "Cutter's Row."
"Ines."
"Ines."
Eleven. Ada had heard that number before, on a ferry, from a man who couldn't remember any of it.
"You haven't told anyone," she said.

"A Register that loses names is not a Register. The Provost would close this office." He paused. "She'd be right to. So I wrote it down where nobody would read it, and I kept the book shut, and I hoped." He looked at the lamp. "That's not a sentence I enjoy saying out loud."
Ada knew that one. Keep the broken thing quiet so nobody takes it off you. She didn't say so.
"Why tell me?"

"Because tonight one came back." His voice had gone very quiet, which she was beginning to learn did not mean calm. "And because you're the only person in Morrow Quay who isn't in this book. Whoever's doing this can't cross you out." He breathed. "For the record, I'd like your help."
"Off the record?"
"Off the record," said Emrys, "please."

He opened the Register and began to turn the pages, to show her. Rope Walk: a blank line. Tanner's Steps: a blank line. Ten of them now, where there had been eleven. At each one he laid his finger on the empty ruling, as if he could keep it warm.
Ada was watching the page he was about to turn.
Halfway down it, a line that wasn't on his list had begun to go grey.
"Emrys."

He looked. The ink was paling as they watched, not smudging, just thinning out, the way the readout thinned in daylight. Ada leaned in to read it, and there was nothing left to read. A ruled line. Brown paper. Blank.
Emrys made a sound she'd never heard from him.
"I knew that," he said. "I've written that name out. I know I have. I..." His hand found his pen, and stopped. "Twelve. Counting Ines."
The lamp hissed. Across the square, the clock did not tick.
Somebody had broken another lantern tonight, while they stood here counting the last one, and the whole town had forgotten someone, and neither of them could say who.
